sentences.text: Guaibasaurus is an extinct basal saurischian dinosaur found in the Late Triassic Caturrita Formation of southern Brazil.
It is described as a small, lightly built dinosaur with a length of about 2 meters.
The femur of specimen UFRGS PV0725T measures 27 centimeters in length.

Basic anatomical features include four fingers in the hand, four toes in the foot with the fifth toe reduced to a single metatarsal, an almost closed acetabulum at the hip joint, and a high medial ridge on a narrow calcaneus.
Estimates for Guaibasaurus size vary, with Gregory S. Paul (2016) suggesting it was about 2 meters long and 10 kg, while Molina-Pérez and Larramendi (2020) estimated it at 3 meters long and 35 kg.
Guaibasaurus was first named by José F. Bonaparte, Jorge Ferigolo, and Ana Maria Ribeiro in 1999, with the type species being Guaibasaurus candelariensis.
There are three recorded fossil occurrences of Guaibasaurus in the Paleobiology Database.
Researchers suggest Guaibasaurus may have rested in a bird-like posture to conserve body heat.
Guaibasaurus is classified in the class Saurischia.
Most analyses classify Guaibasaurus as a sauropodomorph, though some studies suggest it was a theropod.
Recent cladistic analyses disagree on Guaibasaurus classification, with some finding it a basal theropod and others a basal sauropodomorph.
Guaibasaurus is classified in the family Guaibasauridae.
The genus authority for Guaibasaurus is Bonaparte et al., 1999.
The species authority for Guaibasaurus candelariensis is Bonaparte et al., 1999.
Bonaparte and colleagues placed the genus in its own family, Guaibasauridae.
In 2007, Bonaparte and colleagues placed the similar Brazilian dinosaur Saturnalia in the same family, Guaibasauridae.
The parent group of the genus Guaibasaurus is Guaibasauridae.
Specimens date to the early Norian faunal stage of the Late Triassic, found in the lower Caturrita Formation or uppermost Santa Maria 2 Sequence.
Guaibasaurus lived during the Late Triassic, approximately 227.4 to 220.7 million years ago, in what is now South America.
Guaibasaurus lived during the Norian stage, from 227.3 to 205.7 million years ago.
It is debated whether other members of Guaibasauridae, such as Saturnalia, form a clade with Guaibasaurus, as they are generally considered very basal sauropodomorphs.
Bonaparte suggested that these forms might be primitive sauropodomorphs or a group of forms near the common ancestor of sauropodomorphs and theropods.
